newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Run-off likely with 15 contesting Madagascar poll.
newsitem.headline: Run-off likely with 15 contesting Madagascar poll.

text.p: Fifteen candidates will compete in Madagascar's presidential election on Sunday, making a second round run-off between the top two a likely prospect.
Preachers and pharmacists, admirals and Marxists, aristocrats and traders are all vying to take charge of the world's fourth-largest island, its 14 million people and their chronic poverty.
With at least five strong candidates, political analysts doubt that any individual will score the simple majority needed to win on the first ballot.
No date has been set for the run-off if one is needed.
Six million registered voters will cast their ballots at 15,000 stations and officials say they expect the first results on Sunday night after the close of 12 hours' voting at 6 p.m. (1500 GMT).
The police and army chiefs have promised that security will be tight and effective after a mainly peaceful campaign in which one party supporter was killed and one seriously injured.
But official sources said there were still problems distributing voter cards and verifying electoral lists on Saturday. They predicted delays and confusion in come areas.
About 50 foreign electoral observers are in Madagascar but some say they lack the means to do the job properly.
The early poll was forced when former president Albert Zafy was impeached by parliament last July and the constitutional court endorsed the decision in September.
The former French colony has lurched from one political crisis to another since 1993 when a long and bloody battle for democracy ended in triumph and high hopes.
The squabbling has frustrated plans to improve life for the islanders, among the poorest people in the world.

Zafy, in his late sixties and known for his trade-mark straw hat, is a leading candidate on Sunday. So are the former military ruler he defeated in 1993, Didier Ratsiraka, and the current prime minister and interim president, Norbert Ratsirahonana.
U.S.-trained millionaire Herizo Razafimahaleo and Richard Andriamanjato, a Marxist pastor who is speaker of the national assembly, are also expected to score well.

Razafimahaleo, the youngest of the front-runners at 41, hired a helicopter to dash around the island pulling in crowds of mainly young people while the other candidates bounced along pot-holed roads by car.
The high level of support during campaigning for retired admiral Ratsiraka, 59, has surprised observers. He returned from 19 months of voluntary exile in France at the end of September.
He was reviled by many of his people in the early nineties for using the army to resist the pro-democracy movement.

The blackest day in those turbulent years was August 10, 1991, when Ratsiraka ordered troops to fire on a huge crowd of protesters surging towards the presidential palace. The official version at the time said 14 people were killed and hundreds wounded.
